newsitem.title: USA: Rise in teen drug use confirmed by new study.
newsitem.headline: Rise in teen drug use confirmed by new study.

text.p: Illegal drug use and cigarette smoking among teenagers continued to rise in 1996, according to federal officials who unveiled the latest drug survey results Thursday.
The sharpest increases were seen in marijuana and cigarette smoking among eighth and 10th graders. Levels for 12th graders were stable for the first time since 1993.
Among eighth graders, who are 13 or 14 years old, 23 percent reported having tried marijuana at least once. That was up from 19.9 percent in 1995.

And about five percent of high school seniors reported using marijuana every day, according to the annual survey of some 50,000 adolescents conducted by the University of Michigan for the National Institute on Drug Abuse.
Despite all the publicity about teen smoking, the numbers rose again over the past year, for the fifth year in a row.
Twenty-one percent of the eighth graders, 30 percent of the 10th graders and 34 percent of the 12th graders said they were smokers. In contrast, about one in four adults smoke.

The Clinton administration has announced extensive new regulations designed to combat teenage smoking. Some of them are being challenged in court but parts of the new rules are set to go into effect Feb. 28.

On a more encouraging note, the study found there were signs of a very recent drop in use of LSD and inhalants. And while heroin use has risen in the past few years, it still remains quite low among adolescents.

Alcohol use, though unacceptably high to most adults, was also stable, the survey found. About a fifth of 10th graders and nearly a third of high school seniors reported they had "been drunk" at least once in the past month.

"The message of today's Monitoring the Future Survey is unmistakable," Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala told a news conference attended by three cabinet members and White House drug adviser Gen. Barry McCaffrey.
"To parents it says, 'Sit down and talk straight to your children about the dangers of drugs, of alcohol and tobacco.' To young people it says, 'Drugs are illegal, dangerous and wrong,'" she said.

Drug officials readily acknowledge it is difficult to get baby-boomers, who may have used marijuana themselves when they were young, to give their teenage children a clear message that it is dangerous.

"But the dangers of marijuana are real and the research proves it," Shalala said, adding that it harms the brain, heart, lungs and immune system, in addition to being chock-full of cancer-causing compounds.

Illegal drug use was a key theme in the 1996 presidential campaign, with President Clinton on the defensive about rising drug use by teenagers during his first term. Surveys have shown that some of that increase, as well as a softening in youth attitudes toward drugs, began before Clinton took office, although the trend accelerated in his presidency.

In addition two states -- California and Arizona -- recently voted to allow broad access to illegal drugs for medical reasons, a policy that federal officials charge is too loosely defined and basically constitutes legalisation.

A group of West Coast academics said in a statement that data from the survey underscore the need to rethink anti-drug education. They said their research had shown that current drug education programmes, particularly the widespread DARE (Drug Abuse Resistance Education), are ineffective.
Some anti-drug groups have said education is only one component and images in films and other entertainment for teenagers, as well as family messages, are also crucial.
